German gross-net calculator 2026

Gross and net pay in Germany, explained

Payroll tax, Soli, church tax and social contributions for employees in tax year 2026, step by step.

Deutsch

The short version

Your net pay is your gross pay minus four kinds of deductions, all of which your employer withholds and pays on your behalf:

  • Payroll tax (Lohnsteuer), the monthly prepayment of your income tax.
  • Solidarity surcharge (Solidaritätszuschlag, “Soli”), which only higher earners still pay.
  • Church tax (Kirchensteuer), only if you belong to a church that levies it.
  • Social contributions for health, long-term care, pension and unemployment insurance.

For example, with a gross salary of €5,000 a month in tax class 1, no children, age 30, no church tax and the average health insurance rate:

Gross€5,000.00
Payroll tax− €782.41
Health insurance− €437.50
Long-term care− €120.00
Pension− €465.00
Unemployment insurance− €65.00
Net€3,130.09

Up to the contribution caps, social contributions take a fixed share of about 21 to 22 % of your gross pay. Payroll tax is progressive: the more you earn, the larger the share it takes.

Social contributions in 2026

You and your employer each pay about half of every contribution. Pay above the monthly cap is contribution-free, which is why net pay rises faster once your salary passes €5,812.50 and again at €8,450.

InsuranceTotal rateYour shareCap per month
Health14.6 % + Zusatzbeitrag7.3 % + half the Zusatzbeitrag€5,812.50
Long-term care3.6 %1.8 %, or 2.4 % without children€5,812.50
Pension18.6 %9.3 %€8,450
Unemployment2.6 %1.3 %€8,450
  • Zusatzbeitrag: every public health insurer sets its own extra contribution. The 2026 average is 2.9 %, so your share of health insurance is typically 8.75 %. Your insurer’s actual rate is on its website and on your payslip.
  • Care insurance and children: from the month after they turn 23, employees who have never had children pay a 0.6-point surcharge. Parents do not pay it, however old their children are (for step- and adoptive parents, conditions apply). People born before 1940 are also exempt. Parents with two to five children under 25 pay 0.25 points less for each child from the second one.
  • Saxony has a different split for care insurance: employees pay 2.3 % (2.9 % without children), employers less.
  • Private health insurance: you pay your insurer’s premium yourself, and your employer pays half of it as a tax-free subsidy, up to €508.59 for health and €104.63 for care insurance a month in 2026 (€75.56 for care insurance in Saxony).

How payroll tax is calculated

Your employer projects your monthly pay to a full year, subtracts the allowances, applies the income tax tariff and divides the result by twelve. The allowances built into payroll tax are:

  • the employee allowance (Arbeitnehmer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,230 for work expenses,
  • a €36 allowance for special expenses (Sonderausgaben-Pauschbetrag),
  • a lump sum for your pension, health, care and unemployment contributions (Vorsorgepauschale),
  • in tax class 2, the single-parent allowance of €4,260.

The 2026 tariff for a single person, by taxable income:

Taxable income per yearRate on each extra euro
up to €12,3480 % (basic allowance, Grundfreibetrag)
€12,349 to €17,799rising from 14 % to about 24 %
€17,800 to €69,878rising from about 24 % to 42 %
€69,879 to €277,82542 %
from €277,82645 %

These are marginal rates: each one only applies to the part of your income within its band. Your average tax rate is always lower.

Tax classes

ClassFor whom
1Single, divorced or widowed people, and married people who live permanently apart or whose spouse lives outside Germany (with a spouse in the EU or EEA, class 3 can still be possible under certain conditions).
2Single parents who live with their child and with no other adult. Includes the €4,260 single-parent allowance; for each further child the tax office adds €240 on request, which the calculator does not include.
3Married, earning clearly more than your spouse, who then takes class 5. The tariff is applied to half the income and doubled (splitting), so withholding is low.
4Married, both earning about the same. Withholding as in class 1.
5Married, earning clearly less than your spouse in class 3. No basic allowance, so withholding is high.
6A second or further job. No basic allowance, employee allowance or special-expenses allowance.

For married couples, the tax class only changes how much is withheld each month. The actual tax is settled in the joint tax return, so 3/5 and 4/4 lead to the same tax for the year. With 3/5 the tax return is compulsory.

Solidarity surcharge and church tax

The Soli is 5.5 % of your payroll tax, but only once your yearly payroll tax exceeds €20,350 (€40,700 in class 3). Above that threshold it is phased in gradually. In class 1, that means no Soli up to a gross salary of roughly €7,700 a month, and the full 5.5 % from about €11,200.

Church tax is 9 % of your payroll tax, or 8 % in Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria. You only pay it as a member of a church that levies it.

Children do not reduce payroll tax itself, because parents receive child benefit (Kindergeld) instead. They do reduce Soli and church tax, which are calculated as if the child allowances of €9,756 per child (the child allowance plus the allowance for care, education and training) had been deducted. In classes 1 and 2 each child usually counts half, because parents share the allowance.

13th salary, holiday pay, Christmas bonus and other one-off payments

Bonuses such as a 13th salary, holiday pay (Urlaubsgeld) or a Christmas bonus (Weihnachtsgeld) are taxed as one-off payments (sonstige Bezüge). Your employer calculates the tax on your yearly pay with the bonus and without it, and withholds the difference. The bonus is therefore taxed at the marginal rate at the top of your income, or across two bands if it is large, so less of it is left than of a normal monthly salary.

The Soli works differently on a bonus: if your yearly tax including the bonus passes the threshold, the full 5.5 % is withheld on the tax on the bonus, with no phase-in. Your tax return settles the exact amount.

Social contributions on a bonus are only due up to the room left under the contribution cap for the year so far (§ 23a SGB IV). If your monthly salary is already above a cap, the bonus is free of that contribution.

Benefit cards (Sachbezug)

Many employers give a prepaid benefit card. Benefits in kind are tax- and contribution-free up to €50 a month. This is an exemption limit, not an allowance: at €50.01 the whole amount becomes taxable. Some employers pay the tax and contributions on a larger benefit themselves, in which case your net pay is not affected. Your payslip shows which applies.

Why your payslip can differ

  • Your health insurer’s Zusatzbeitrag is above or below the 2.9 % average.
  • You have an allowance registered with the tax office (Freibetrag), or you and your spouse use the factor method.
  • Your pay includes a company pension (bAV) by salary conversion, capital-forming benefits (VWL), a company car or other benefits.
  • You earn €2,000 a month or less: from €603.01 midijob rules lower your contributions, and up to €603 a minijob has its own rules.
  • Deductions after net pay, such as the canteen, reduce the amount paid out but not your net pay.

Payroll tax is a prepayment. Your actual income tax is settled in your tax return, where work expenses above €1,230, for example, can lead to a refund.

How exact is the calculator?

Payroll tax, Soli and church tax follow the official 2026 payroll tax algorithm of the German Ministry of Finance (BMF Programmablaufplan), the same one payroll software uses, and are tested against the ministry’s own calculator. Everything runs in your browser, and nothing you enter leaves the page.

This page explains the general rules. It is not tax or legal advice, and all figures are without guarantee.
